clue.text: An extra actor has a point to being sort of pure, but hasn't anything to say, which is very, very good!

parts.note: S, south, is one of the compass points

indicators.note: a sort of pure is a loose version of the word, so its letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A walk-on actor who is somehow pure and never speaks turns out to be wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges the word into UPER. The opening also hints at the answer another way: an extra with no lines is a super, short for supernumerary.
explanation.definitionFit: Super is an informal adjective of praise meaning excellent or first-rate.

clue.text: Where bands play and newspapers are sold.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bandstands, where a band performs
second meaning: newsstands, stalls that sell papers

explanation.walkthrough: Each half is a kind of stand: the bandstand in a park and the newsstand on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand is a raised structure or stall, as in bandstand for musicians and newsstand for paper sellers.

clue.text: Being somewhat la-di-da is one point to get nosy about.

indicators.note: about puts the nosy word around the other letters

parts.note: to pry is to be nosy
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A snooty person is a reason for others to snoop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' marks the container, with the nosy word on the outside. La-di-da means affectedly refined or genteel.
explanation.definitionFit: Prissy means fussily prim and proper, close to the affected refinement of la-di-da.

clue.text: Unusual prices for directions to the cook.

indicators.note: unusual prices are the word in an odd order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word printed is prices, but the anagram needs a second E in place of its S: the setter's slip, so the letters are taken as the clue should have read

explanation.surface: Odd costs are passed on to the kitchen as instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' signals an anagram of PRICES, but those letters give RECIPS, not the answer: the setter's fodder is one letter out, an S where a second E is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A recipe is the set of instructions telling a cook how to prepare a dish.

clue.text: A bit on the lemony side–you get to holler with nothing but a final hope!

definitions.text: A bit on the lemony side

parts.note: to holler is to yell
O looks like zero, nothing
a wish is a hope, here the last piece of the answer

explanation.surface: Something slightly sour-tasting makes you shout with only one last hope left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lemony' suggests taste, but here it is lemon as a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemons are yellow, so something slightly lemon-coloured is tinged with that colour; the -ish suffix gives the hedge.

clue.text: What happens when you're sworn to secrecy? There's no way of knowing!

definitions.text: What happens when you're sworn to secrecy
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: you are never able to tell anyone
second meaning: the idiom for something unpredictable

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for unpredictability also describes, word for word, a person bound to keep a secret.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says an outcome is uncertain, matching the impossibility of knowing it in advance.

clue.text: What some writers go around in?

definitions.text: What some writers go around in?

parts.words: What some writers go around in?
parts.note: a cryptic definition: authors' social groups pictured as rings they travel round

explanation.walkthrough: 'go around in' suggests clothing or vehicles; the joke is that writers' social sets are called circles.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary circles are groups of authors and critics who mix socially and discuss books.

clue.text: Given certain freedom, there's no getting up quietly, with a part to play.

indicators.note: in a down answer, getting up means the word no is read from the bottom up

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for quiet
a role is an actor's part

explanation.surface: A released prisoner who will not rise in silence, but has a role to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting up' turns NO into ON in this down entry, followed by P, A and ROLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner on parole is released early under conditions, a limited and conditional liberty.

clue.text: Where you don't want to be during a hurricane, or get a sock this way.

definitions.text: Where you don't want to be during a hurricane
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the eye is the centre of the storm
second meaning: a punch that lands on the eye

explanation.walkthrough: The storm's centre and a punch to the face share one phrase; a sock here is a punch, not clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurricane's eye is its central region, and a blow to the eye is a punch landed there.

clue.text: A fancy name for a place to stay when broken-down hotels are located on the short railway line.

definitions.text: A fancy name for a place to stay

indicators.note: in a down answer, the hotels sit on top of the railway, so it comes after them
broken-down hotels are the word knocked apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Run-down hotels beside a branch line pass themselves off grandly as inns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken-down' makes HOSTEL; in a down entry, 'are located on' puts that above the railway, so the railway comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostelry is a rather grand or jocular word for an inn or pub, a place offering lodging.

clue.text: A famous battle, where you got a drink before the king and queen.

parts.note: gin is an alcoholic drink
a royal court is the king and queen with their household

explanation.surface: A battlefield story about stopping for a drink before meeting royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Agincourt was the 1415 victory of Henry V's English army over the French, one of history's best-known battles.

clue.text: Heads you get served these…

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the tops of heads
second meaning: pâtés are savoury pastes served as a starter

explanation.walkthrough: The same letters spell an old word for heads and, with accents, the French meat pastes; the ellipsis runs the clue into the next one.
explanation.definitionFit: A pate is the crown of the head, while pâté is a spread of meat or fish served on toast.

clue.text: …and possibly said to go very quietly with something on the side of your head, and totally vanish!

indicators.note: possibly said is one possible rearrangement of the word, so its letters are mixed

parts.note: pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quiet

parts.words: something on the side of your head
parts.note: an ear sits on each side of the head

explanation.surface: Continuing from the heads: whispering beside someone's ear before vanishing completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' makes DISA; 'very quietly' is the pianissimo marking in sheet music.
explanation.definitionFit: To disappear is to pass out of sight completely, so it matches vanishing.

clue.text: An administrative officer is ever at sea, at some point.

indicators.note: something at sea is confused, so the letters of the word are scrambled

parts.note: E, east, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A council official is always away sailing at some time or other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' mixes EVER into REEV, and the compass point E ends it. A reeve was a medieval English local official, such as a manor's steward.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local magistrate or steward who administered a district or estate for the lord or king.

clue.text: American novel. Maybe bucks at one point, and gets chicken, possibly!

parts.note: bucks are male deer, so deer is the wider class
S, south, is a compass point
a laying hen is a layer, one example of a chicken

explanation.surface: A book review imagines male animals bolting and turning cowardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bucks' and 'chicken' look like money and cowardice; here they are a male deer and an egg-laying hen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Deerslayer is James Fenimore Cooper's 1841 frontier novel, one of the Leatherstocking Tales.

clue.text: Take little notice, but it's a way to get away around it, with a little fling!

indicators.note: the escape route goes around the notice, which it names

parts.note: an escape is a means of getting away
an ad is a small advertisement or notice

explanation.surface: Ignore a minor warning and slip off for a brief wild time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around it' marks the container, the 'it' pointing back to the little notice, which goes inside the way to get away.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a daring or carefree adventure, a brief spree of the kind called a fling.

clue.text: One who makes fun of things being equal to somewhat of a poet.

definitions.text: One who makes fun of things

parts.note: at par means equal in value
an odist writes odes, one kind of poet

explanation.surface: A satirist who is a poet's equal, in a fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: PAR is equality, as in 'on a par'; an odist writes odes.
explanation.definitionFit: A parodist imitates a style or work in an exaggerated way for comic effect, mocking it.

clue.text: To give rise to no coca is bad.

indicators.note: bad here means jumbled, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that going without the drink causes trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: To occasion something is to cause or bring it about, which is what giving rise to it means.

clue.text: A fowl made ready for the grill. (You get to mend a number in your little stocking!)

definitions.text: A fowl made ready for the grill

indicators.note: in places the mending piece and number within the short stocking

parts.note: a sock is a short stocking
to patch is to mend
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: A cooking note with a darning aside about patching a numbered sock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks the container; the sock is split after its first letter to take the mend and the number.
explanation.definitionFit: A spatchcock is a bird split open and flattened so it can be grilled quickly.

clue.text: The wrong shapes for certain aspects of the moon.

indicators.note: the wrong shapes are the word in the wrong order, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mistaken outlines account for the moon's different appearances.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunar phases are the changing appearances of the moon, such as crescent and full.

clue.text: Erect, I scrambled to repeat the lesson.

indicators.note: scrambled means the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A pupil, standing up in confusion, recites the lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: To recite is to say aloud from memory, as a pupil repeats a lesson to the teacher.

clue.text: A short way with the old way plays are put on.

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
the aged are the old

explanation.surface: A theatre note on how plays are mounted on a little street.
explanation.walkthrough: ST and AGED join.
explanation.definitionFit: A staged play is one produced and performed in a theatre, which is how plays are put on.

clue.text: A pleasant smell, as some signs could say in Italy.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sweet or appetising scent

definitions.text: as some signs could say in Italy
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Italian road signs read 'a Roma', to Rome

explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words, the answer is Italian for 'to Rome', as on a road sign pointing to the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: An aroma is a distinctive, usually agreeable, odour such as that of coffee or baking.

clue.text: There's a point to the worst sort of direction.

parts.note: N, north, is a compass point

indicators.note: a sort of the worst is a loose version of those words, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumble that some directions are the worst kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges THE WORST into ORTHWEST, after the point N.
explanation.definitionFit: Northwest is a compass bearing midway between north and west.

clue.text: You can't say there's no excuse for this!

definitions.text: You can't say there's no excuse for this!

parts.words: You can't say there's no excuse for this!
parts.note: a cryptic definition: the answer is itself an excuse, so no excuse can be lacking for it

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a scolding, but read literally it describes the very thing that is an excuse.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere, used as an excuse to avoid blame.

clue.text: An irregular lien with sharp pain at the end for signing up.

indicators.note: says the sharp pain goes after the rearranged letters
an irregular lien is the word put out of order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a sting is a sharp pain

explanation.surface: Enrolling brings an odd legal claim and a sting at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'irregular' makes ENLI and 'at the end' places the sharp pain last. A lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid.
explanation.definitionFit: Enlisting is joining up, especially enrolling in the armed forces.

clue.text: Gets terribly mixed up with possibly ten ways of looking at things.

indicators.note: possibly ten is one possible rearrangement of the word, so its letters are mixed

parts.note: an angle is a point of view on a matter

explanation.surface: Someone gets confused by ten different viewpoints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' makes ENT; 'terribly mixed up' looks like anagram signalling too, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To entangle is to twist together or embroil, so it gets things thoroughly tangled.

clue.text: The hero's charger in a short way, when the river flows back.

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: the river flowing back means its name is read backwards

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another between Wales and England

explanation.surface: A hero's warhorse on a short street as a river reverses its flow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flows back' makes EED; 'charger' is the old word for a warhorse, not an electrical device.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger is a cavalry horse, and steed is the literary word for a spirited riding horse.
